Here's a little essay that surfaced when I asked myself the same question:

**The Last Eclipse**

Totality begins with silence. Birds stop singing mid-phrase and head for their roosts, confused by dusk arriving four hours early. The temperature falls several degrees in minutes. Streetlights tick on in distant towns. Around the entire horizon runs a pale band of gold—the light of somewhere else, somewhere outside the shadow you're standing in—as if sunset were happening in all directions at once. Then, through a gap in the clouds or behind the last sliver of sun, appears the thing people travel across continents to see: the corona, the sun's ghostly outer atmosphere, hanging in the dark like silver smoke.

Almost nobody who sees it knows how lucky they are to be looking.

Consider the numbers. The sun is about four hundred times wider than the moon. It also happens to sit, at this particular moment in cosmic history, about four hundred times farther away. Divide one by the other and they resolve to exactly the same size in our sky—which is the only reason the moon can cover the sun completely, erasing its glare, unveiling the corona. This alignment isn't physical law or fate. It's an accident of timing. A coin held at arm's length covers either one. Nothing about ourselves explains the coincidence except this: we happen to be alive while it holds.

It won't hold. Tidal friction means every wave, every dragging bulge of ocean beneath the passing moon, acts as a brake on Earth's spin—and that stolen momentum gets paid into the moon's orbit, nudging it outward about 3.8 centimeters a year. We know the number precisely because astronauts left mirror arrays up there, and observatories still bounce lasers off them nightly, tracking the drift in millimeters. The moon buys its slow escape with our afternoons: Earth's days are stretching by a couple of milliseconds per century.

Run the clock forward and the geometry quietly fails. The moon's disk shrinks in the sky year by year until it can no longer swallow the sun whole. Eclipses don't stop; they degrade. They become rings of fire, annular events where a blazing ring escapes around the rim and the corona drowns in daylight again. Estimates vary, but most put the last total solar eclipse somewhere around six hundred million years from now. Totality, in other words, is not a permanent feature of the universe. It's a phenomenon with a lifespan—born shortly after the impact that created the moon, when the disk hung huge and terrifying in a faster sky, fated to die long before the sun does. Like a species, it arises, flourishes in a niche, and vanishes when conditions change.

And its niche is *now*. Of everything totality's lifetime contains, we live in the heart of it.

There's one more quiet loss hiding in that fact. On an ordinary day, the corona is absolutely invisible—the scattered blue of our own atmosphere is millions of times brighter than the sun's thin outer air. For billions of years, the only place in the universe to see the corona with naked eyes was standing inside the moon's shadow, on Earth, for those few minutes. inventors eventually built instruments to fake totality, but before that, and after, it remains a view rationed out in seconds.

So perhaps that's part of why we photograph eclipses so obsessively. Somewhere down the timeline, someone or something will know the perfect ones only as archives: images of a branching silver corona above a dark landscape, the longest sunset ever painted. There's something tender about recording a wonder for successors who can never stand inside it. And something bracing, too—a reminder that even the sky's oldest parlor tricks come with expiry dates. The geometry is holding. Go stand in the shadow while the shadow still exists.
